sections.title: Anti-Derivatives (Indefinite Integrals)
sections.content: Integration is the reverse process of differentiation. If d/dx [F(x)] = f(x), then the integral of f(x) w.r.t x is F(x) + C, where C is the constant of integration. It represents a family of parallel curves.

sections.title: Standard Integral Formulas
sections.content: Memorize basics: ∫x^n dx = [x^(n+1)]/(n+1) (n ≠ -1). ∫(1/x) dx = ln|x|. ∫e^x dx = e^x. ∫sin(x) dx = -cos(x). ∫cos(x) dx = sin(x). ∫sec^2(x) dx = tan(x).

sections.title: Algebra of Integrals
sections.content: Integrals are linear: ∫[a*f(x) ± b*g(x)] dx = a*∫f(x) dx ± b*∫g(x) dx. However, there is NO direct product or quotient rule like in differentiation; specific methods must be applied.

sections.title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Definite Integrals)
sections.content: Definite integrals have upper (b) and lower (a) limits and do not require '+ C'. ∫f(x) dx from a to b = F(b) - F(a). It represents the algebraic sum of areas between the curve and the x-axis.

sections.title: Basic Area Under Curve (AUC)
sections.content: Area bounded by y = f(x), the x-axis, and lines x = a, x = b is ∫|f(x)| dx from a to b. If the curve is below the x-axis, the integral evaluates to a negative number, so take the absolute value for geometric area.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
1) Forgetting the constant of integration '+ C' in indefinite integrals.
2) Applying the power rule to ∫(1/x) dx instead of using ln|x|.
3) Forgetting to take the modulus in AUC when the curve dips below the x-axis.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 1 establishes integration as reverse differentiation. Master the standard formulas, apply limits to find exact numerical values (Definite), and understand the geometric meaning of integrals as area.

tricks.title: Reverse Differentiation Check
tricks.explanation: To verify if your indefinite integral is correct, simply differentiate your answer. If you get the original integrand, you are 100% correct.
tricks.example: ∫sec(x)tan(x) dx = sec(x) + C. Differentiating sec(x) gives sec(x)tan(x).

tricks.title: Linear Substitution Shortcut
tricks.explanation: If ∫f(x) dx = F(x) + C, then ∫f(ax + b) dx = F(ax + b)/a + C. Just divide by the coefficient of x.

tricks.title: f'(x) / f(x) Shortcut
tricks.explanation: If the numerator is the exact derivative of the denominator, the integral is simply the natural log of the denominator.

tricks.title: Trig Power Reduction
tricks.explanation: Never integrate sin^2(x) or cos^2(x) directly. Always convert them using double angle formulas.
tricks.example: sin^2(x) = (1 - cos(2x))/2. Now integrate 1/2 and cos(2x)/2 separately.

tricks.title: Geometric Definite Integrals
tricks.explanation: If the function forms a standard geometric shape (line, circle, semicircle), don't integrate! Just calculate the area geometrically.
tricks.example: ∫√(a^2 - x^2) dx from 0 to a is a quarter circle. Area = (π*a^2)/4.

tricks.title: Option Elimination via '+ C'
tricks.explanation: In multiple-choice questions, sometimes substituting x = 0 or x = 1 into the differentiated options quickly eliminates wrong answers without actually integrating.
tricks.example: Differentiate options and match with the given question function.
